units.intro: Atoms stick because electrons are shared or transferred.

cards.title: 2.1 Forces of Attractions
body: Chemical bonds are the forces of attraction that hold atoms together: can be described as attractive forces.
Intramolecular bonds refer to the forces of attraction that hold atoms together within a molecule.
Generally, intramolecular forces are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Polar and Non polar Covalent Bonds
body: A Polar covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the electrons are not equally shared.
The more electronegative atom attracts the shared electron pairs more than the one with less electronegative value.
The Cl atom has the higher electronegativity so the electrons are drawn more towards the Cl atom and away from the H atom.
Since electrons carry a negative charge, this gives the Cl atom a partial negative charge.

A dative bond requires an electron pair donor (with a lone pair) and an acceptor (with an empty orbital).

cards.title: 2.3 Intermolecular Forces of Attraction
body: The positive and negative poles of the polar liquid attract the negative and positive ions of the ionic substance, respectively.
The strength of these interactions depends on the charge and the size of the ion and on the magnitude of polarity and size of the dipole.
Dipole-Dipole forces These forces occur when polar molecules arrange themselves such that their oppositely charged ends can attract each other.
The hydrogen atom has a slightly positive charge and the chlorine atom has a slightly negative charge.
Because of the force of attraction between oppositely charged particles, there is a small dipole-dipole force of attraction between adjacent HCl molecules.

cards.title: Intermolecular Forces of Attraction
body: Between molecules: weak intermolecular forces (including hydrogen bonding in water, which is why water is liquid and has a high boiling point for such a small molecule).

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Ionic = I own it (transfer). Covalent = co-own (share). Metallic = mobile sea. “Giant covalent does not dissolve and does not melt easily.”

cards.title: How to classify an unknown solid
body: Ask four school tests: melting point high or low? Does the solid conduct? Does the melt/solution conduct? Does it dissolve in water? High melt + conducts only when molten/dissolved → ionic. High melt + never conducts + insoluble → giant covalent. Low melt + never conducts → simple molecular. Conducts as a solid and bends → metal.

Dot-and-cross: metals lose until they look noble; non-metals gain or share until they look noble. MgCl₂ needs two Cl because Mg gives two electrons. Covalent pairs sit between symbols; leftover dots are lone pairs. Lone pairs push — that is why water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal (named properly in Grade 12).

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong intermolecular force, not a fourth primary bond. It explains water’s high boiling point, ice floating, and DNA later. When water boils you break H-bonds between molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule — if you broke those you would make hydrogen and oxygen gases.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following substances consists of completely nonpolar covalent bonds?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify bond type of homonuclear diatomic molecules**
Homonuclear diatomic molecules contain two identical nonmetal atoms.

**Step 2: Apply electronegativity values**
For $$\text{Cl}_2$$, the electronegativity difference is:
$$\Delta\text{EN} = \text{EN of Cl} - \text{EN of Cl} = 3.0 - 3.0 = 0.0$$
Since the sharing of electrons is perfectly equal, the bonds are entirely nonpolar covalent.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The nonpolar covalent substance is **$$\text{Cl}_2$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following lists intermolecular forces in the correct order of increasing attractive strength?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare relative strengths of intermolecular forces**
*   London dispersion forces (caused by temporary fluctuations in electron clouds) are the weakest.
*   Dipole-dipole forces (between permanent polar molecules) are of intermediate strength.
*   Hydrogen bonding (a exceptionally strong, unique dipole-dipole attraction involving FON) is the strongest of these three.

**Step 2: Final Answer**
The correct increasing order is **London dispersion < dipole-dipole < Hydrogen bonding**.

glossary.meaning: Metallic bonding refers to the interaction between the delocalized electrons and the positive metal ions.
A Polar covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the electrons are not equally shared.
Electronegativity is the attractive power of an atom for shared electron pairs.

tips.text: Covalent bonds are formed by the sharing of electrons, which commonly occurs when two nonmetals bond together.
A coordinate covalent bond, also called a dative bond, is a force of attraction resulting from the sharing of a lone pair of electrons from one atom with another atom.
Metallic bonding refers to the interaction between the delocalized electrons and the positive metal ions.

The physical properties of metals, electrical conductivity, high melting and boiling point, lustre, malleability and ductility are mainly due to the delocalized electrons. These attractive forces occur when an ionic substance dissolves in a polar liquid, e.g.
The positive and negative poles of the polar liquid attract the negative and positive ions of the ionic substance, respectively.
